writing.topic: Write an e-mail to a German friend about last weekend: where you went, who you were with, what you did and what you thought of it. Finish by asking your friend one question about their weekend.
writing.practisePoints[0]: an informal greeting (Hallo / Liebe / Lieber) and an informal sign-off
writing.practisePoints[1]: tell it in the Perfekt: ich habe … gemacht, ich bin … gefahren
writing.practisePoints[2]: use sein for going and coming (ich bin gefahren, wir sind gegangen) and haben for the rest
writing.practisePoints[3]: say when, with at least two time expressions (am Samstag, am Nachmittag, danach)
writing.practisePoints[4]: say what you thought of it, with one opinion sentence
writing.practisePoints[5]: end with one question to your friend
writing.scoringCriteria[0]: all four content points are there: where, with whom, what you did, what you thought of it
writing.scoringCriteria[1]: the e-mail reads as a message to a friend, with du and an informal greeting
writing.scoringCriteria[2]: it ends with one question about the friend's weekend
help.hook: Tell a friend about your weekend in German, and have your own AI correct it.
help.intro: You have drilled the Perfekt gap by gap; now you write a whole e-mail with it. You write the message here in the box, and the app builds a correction request that carries your own text. You paste that into your own AI, it corrects what you actually wrote, and you bring the score back. The fixes are saved as your next things to work on. Aim for 200 to 500 characters, about the length of a real message to a friend. The one thing that will cost you marks is slipping into the present tense halfway through, so check every verb before you send it.
help.tips[0].title: A whole message in the Perfekt
help.tips[0].text: When you tell someone what you did, German uses the Perfekt almost everywhere: haben or sein in second position, the Partizip II at the very end. Keep it up for the whole message. One present-tense sentence in the middle makes the reader think you have moved back to today.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: On Saturday I visited my sister.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: We went into town together and watched a film.
help.tips[0].trap: The participle goes last, after everything else: „Ich habe am Sonntag lange geschlafen“, not „Ich habe geschlafen am Sonntag“.
help.tips[0].check.why: spielen takes haben, and the participle gespielt stays at the end.
help.tips[1].title: sein for going, haben for the rest
help.tips[1].text: Verbs of going and coming take sein: ich bin gefahren, gegangen, geflogen, gekommen, geblieben. Almost everything else takes haben. If you can picture yourself moving from one place to another, reach for bin.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: I travelled to Hamburg on Friday.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: We stayed in the cafe for a long time and talked a lot.
help.tips[1].trap: bleiben takes sein although nobody moves anywhere: ich bin geblieben.
help.tips[1].check.q: Wir ____ am Sonntag ins Kino gegangen.
help.tips[1].check.why: gehen is a verb of movement, so its Perfekt is formed with sein.
help.tips[2].title: Order the weekend with zuerst, dann, danach
help.tips[2].text: A message about your weekend is easier to read, and easier to write, if you walk through it in order. Zuerst … dann … danach … am Abend. Each of those can start the sentence, and when it does, the verb follows it straight away.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: First we had breakfast, then we drove to the lake.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: Afterwards I was very tired, but it was fun.
help.tips[2].check.why: After an opening word like dann the verb comes next, then the subject.
help.tips[2].visual.moves[0].label: Greeting
help.tips[2].visual.moves[3].label: Ask back
help.remember[0]: Perfekt all the way through: haben or sein in second place, Partizip II at the end.
help.remember[1]: sein for going and coming (gefahren, gegangen, geblieben); haben for the rest.
help.remember[2]: war and hatte stay simple: Es war schön, Ich hatte keine Zeit.
help.remember[3]: Informal frame: Hallo Max, … then Liebe Grüße and your name.
help.exam: A short e-mail about what you did is one of the written tasks the A2 certificate sets, and the message you will actually send most often.
help.mistakes[0].why: spielen takes haben, and the participle goes last.
help.mistakes[1].why: fahren is movement, so it takes sein.
help.mistakes[2].why: After an opening time phrase the verb comes second, before the subject.
help.mistakes[3].why: The question belongs before the sign-off, and the sign-off takes no comma.
help.vocab[5].en: to be fun (Das hat Spaß gemacht)
